title: TB9-25559
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX, (Associate Appellant) XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX (Minor Appellants), citizens of Nigeria, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated August 30, 2019, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX, (Associate Appellant) XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX (Minor Appellants), citizens of Nigeria, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated August 30, 2019, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses this appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD. The Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
The Appellants fear being harmed or killed by Fulani herdsmen who want to graze their cattle on the Appellants' farmland.

The Appellants' farm is located in XXXX XXXX Benue state, Nigeria. On XXXX XXXX 2017 their farm was attacked by Fulani herdsmen and the house was burned down. The Appellants fled to XXXX and reported the incident to police. On XXXX XXXX 2017 the Principal Appellant was XXXX on his way home from work and held for several days before being rescued by hunters or vigilantes.
The Principal Appellant also fears because he is the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in XXXX of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The other members were all kidnapped and murdered.
The Associate Appellant's and the Minor Appellants' claims are based on the Principal Appellant's claim. The Principal Appellant acted as designated representative for the Minor Appellants.
The Appellants fled Nigeria for the United States on XXXX XXXX 2018. They came to Canada and claimed refugee status on XXXX XXXX 2018.
The Appellants filed their Basis of Claim (BOC) forms on 23 May 2018. The Principal Appellant filed an amendment to his BOC narrative on 21 January 2018.
I have considered the whole of the Record to determine whether the RPD's decision is correct on questions of law, fact or mixed law and fact.1

I have reviewed the audio recording of the hearing, the documents filed by the Appellants, the objective documentation and counsel's submissions. Having done so, I determine the RPD had no meaningful advantage over the RAD in evaluating this evidence. I find I owe no deference to the RPD's findings.

The RPD determined the Principal Appellant had constructed the kidnapping allegation in order to bolster his claim. It also found the Principal Appellant's testimony lacked credibility with regard to his assertion that the Fulani had the means to track him anywhere in Nigeria. The RPD found that viable Internal Flight Alternatives (IFA) existed in Abuja or Port Harcourt. Finally, the RPD did not accept the Appellants' explanation for failure to claim in the United Sates.

The Appellants raise the following grounds of appeal which I have reordered and revised: 1. The Appellants provided a reasonable explanation for not seeking protection in the United States; 2. The RPD erred in its assessment of the Principal Appellant's credibility; 3. The RPD erred in its assessment of IFA - both with regard to the possibility of being persecuted and the reasonableness of the proposed IFA.

The Appellants seeks to have a psychologist's report2 and an Immigration and Refugee Board Response to Information Request3 admitted as new evidence. I have determined only the psychologist's report is admissible.

In determining whether to admit new evidence the RAD must apply the provisions of s.110(4) of IRPA.4 I must consider whether the evidence arose after the rejection of the claim, or whether it was not reasonably available at the time of the rejection, or whether the Appellants could not reasonably have been expected under the circumstances to have presented the evidence at the time of the rejection.
If one of these conditions is met, I must then go on to consider whether this evidence is credible, relevant and new,5 failing which, the evidence cannot be admitted.
The Appellants make no submissions as to how this evidence meets any of the applicable criteria.

The RIR the Appellants seek to admit is already a part of the Record and was included in the National Document Package (NDP) that was entered into evidence at the RPD hearing.6 It is therefore not necessary to consider its admission as new evidence.

The psychologist's report meets the criteria of section 110(4). The report is dated XXXX XXXX 2019 and therefore was clearly not available at the time the Appellants' claims were rejected on 30 August 2019. I have no reason to question the report's credibility as it relates to its source and circumstance. Despite the lack of submissions, I find the report is new information which could be relevant to the assessment of the testimony provided by the Principal Appellant. The psychologist's report will therefore be admitted.

Section 110(6) of Immigration and Refugee Protection Act7 provides that the RAD may hold a hearing where new evidence has been admitted. The new evidence must raise a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellants which is both central to, and, if accepted, would justify allowing or denying, the Appellants' claim.
The only new evidence admitted is the psychologist's report. The Appellants make no arguments as to how the requirements of section 110(6) are met.

I find that the report does not raise an issue which is central to the Appellants' claim. This is because the report is based on self-reporting by the Principal Appellant. It is therefore not capable of independently corroborating or proving the truth of the Principal Appellant's specific allegations.

While I note that the report indicates that the Principal Appellant may have some difficulty testifying, the RPD did not base its credibility finding on such difficulties. Rather, the RPD found the Principal Appellant constructed a kidnapping allegation in his amended BOC in order to bolster his claim. The basis for this finding was that the kidnapping allegation had not been included in the Principal Appellants' original BOC. The report has no bearing on this finding.
The Appellants' request for an oral hearing is therefore denied.

I find the RPD did err in its assessment of the Appellant's credibility and failure to claim in the United States. However, the determinative issue in this appeal is the existence of an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA). I find that a viable IFA exists for the Appellants in Abuja. The appeal is therefore rejected. Failure to claim in the Unites States
The Appellants' failure to claim protection in the United States may be a factor in assessing the Appellants' subjective fear but is not in itself determinative.8

The Appellants sought protection within a few days of departure from Nigeria. Whether they always intended to come to Canada or made the decision en route is irrelevant as it is clear their intention was to leave Nigeria permanently and seek protection.
I find the two days the Appellants spent in the United States insufficient to create an expectation that they would seek protection during that stay.9
I therefore find the RPD erred when it found that the failure to claim in the United States was determinative. Credibility of Kidnapping allegation
I find the RPD erred when it determined that the kidnapping allegation was fabricated by the Principal Appellant for the purposes of strengthening the Appellants' claim.

The Appellants argue the documentary evidence and oral testimony showed that the kidnapping "could have" happened.10 The Appellants further argue that the RPD was overzealous and over-vigilant in its examination of the Appellants' testimony.11
The Appellants do not identify which document or portion of testimony they refer to.

While the Appellants' submitted several documents in support of their claim, only two of these, the Affidavits from the Principal Appellant's pastor12 and supervisor13 mention the alleged kidnapping. Both of these documents post-date the amendment of the Principal Appellant's BOC narrative. Both documents indicate that the affiants had been informed of the kidnapping by the Principal Appellant himself. They therefore do not provide any independent verification of the Principal Appellant's allegations.

On the other hand, the RPD correctly notes in its reasons that the allegation of kidnapping was omitted from the original BOC14 and only added in the amended narrative.15 I agree that the kidnapping allegation was clearly central to the Appellants' claim.

The RPD found that, "The explanation provided for this central omission was that he had engaged another lawyer prior to his current lawyer who had instructed him to be brief does not persuade the panel that this fact (the kidnapping) could truthful or trustworthy...". 16 Here the RPD is clearly indicating that this central omission of the kidnapping from the first BOC was put to the Principal Appellant.

However, a review of the audio recording of the RPD hearing shows that the Principal Appellant was never specifically confronted with this omission. On the contrary, the RPD's questioning on the differences between the two BOCs was very general in nature: Presiding Member: Can you tell me something, why was the first BOC so short and so much detail provided in your second BOC? Principal Appellant: ... the first lawyer I had said I should just summarize whatever stories I want to tell. ... just the summary of it. And I told my wife ... like, look, most times we get to see her, its like, um, maybe she's supposed to spend like an hour with us but she keeps bumping in and bumping out attending to two other, three, four, five clients at the same time. So to me I felt we were not being listened to more ... she said she just wanted a summary, she was not doing, was not necessary, have to be ... (inaudible) summary ... so when I did that, I submitted to her, "Is this ok?', she said, "Its ok". So not until I ... Presiding Member: And who was that lawyer? ... Ok - so she just asked you to give a brief accounting. Principal Appellant: Yeah. Presiding Member: And now you have a different lawyer. Principal Appellant: Yeah. Presiding Member: Who has asked you for some details, I gather. Principal Appellant: (inaudible) ... when I presented to him and he said no, no, no, no, no, no that this is not the template for me to use. That in the fist instance the introduction of myself and my family got to be in there. Presiding Member: That's fine, that's fine. And he told you give details of your story. Principal Appellant: Yeah, I need to remember those dates these things happened and all that. Presiding Member: Yeah. Yeah, That's fine. Thank you.

No further questions were asked with regard to the differences between the two BOCs. The Principal Appellant was never asked why he had omitted the kidnapping incident in the original version. Even though it is likely that the Principal Appellant would have given the same answer, I find the RPD did not, as it indicates in its reasons, put this omission to him. The RPD therefore, based its central credibility finding on a question that was not in fact put to the Principal Appellant. I find that, even though it would have been open to the RPD to reject this explanation for the omission, the RPD erred by indicating it had put the omission to the Principal Appellant when in fact it had not done so. The RPD's negative credibility finding therefore cannot stand. Internal Flight Alternative

Even if the Appellants were credibile with regard to the central allegations of their claim, I find the RPD correctly determined that Port Harcourt would provide a viable internal flight alternative. Having found a viable IFA in Port Harcourt, there is no reason for me to separately assess Abuja.

The test for assessing an IFA consists of two parts:17 (1) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. (2) Moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for her to seek refuge there.18
Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the Appellants have a viable IFA.

The Appellants bear the onus of adducing evidence to show, on a balance of probabilities, that a serious possibility of harm exists in the proposed IFA and that the proposed IFA is unreasonable in all the circumstances.
In coming to this decision, I have considered the Jurisprudential Guide with regard to the existence of a possible IFA in Nigeria for persons who fear non-state actors.19

With regard to the first prong of the test, the RPD found, in essence, there was no objective evidence which showed that Fulani herdsman were able to track down and target opponents anywhere in Nigeria.

The Appellants argue that the inability to find evidence of such Fulani activity is because this is a "new phenomenon" and that "... sufficient documents were produced to show the herdsman and Boko Haram activities in Nigeria".20 The Appellants do not identify which documents they are referring to.

The Appellants argue the RPD failed to conduct a thorough analysis of their subjective fear since the Appellants stated "... Abuja or Port Harcourt are not reasonable IFAs for them for a number of reasons."21 I have already determined that subjective fear is not determinative in this case. However, I am prepared to accept, for purposes of this analysis, that the Appellants do fear Fulani herdsman. The question is whether the Fulani would have the means or motivation to track down and harm the Appellants in Port Harcourt.

Fulani herdsmen are nomadic pastoralists and mostly Muslim. The evidence shows the conflict between herders and farmers in Nigeria is widespread, affecting many states. Civilians on both sides of the conflict have been targeted and killed.22 Some sources assert the reason behind the conflict is an expansionist Islamic policy to evict Christian farmers from their lands. However, more neutral sources, such as UNHCR, indicate the conflict is basically one of co-existence, driven by a lack of resources, desertification, ''ambiguous'' land legislation, and a ''weak'' rule of law."23

The BBC reports that, "... while talks of 'genocide against Christians' is a widely touted refrain, it falls short of being supported by facts; there have been many killings on both sides in this conflict.'"24

Although the conflict has escalated in recent years,25 I see no basis for the Appellants' assertion that information on the current activities of Fulani herdsmen is not available. Extensive information on the conflict and the Fulani exists in the sources referenced here - all of which formed a part of the Record before the RPD. What is missing from these sources is any mention of Fulani herdsmen tracking individuals from state to state as the Appellants allege. Instead, the sources provide details of attacks against primarily rural communities as opposed to specific individuals. While I am prepared to accept that the Appellants could be targeted by Fulani herdsmen if they occupied their farm as part of the overall conflict between farmers and pastoralists over land resources, this does not show that the herdsmen would be willing or able to pursue them to Port Harcourt.

While I agree with the Appellants that the Principal Appellant never specifically testified that Fulani herdsmen would be able to track him through official registers or that they operate at international airports, the Principal Appellant nonetheless testified at various points that the Fulani herdsmen had a network throughout the country, that they were everywhere, that they are connected to the government, connected to ritualists, connected to Boko Haram and, in essence, that they could use technology to easily monitor and track the Appellants.26

I find the Principal Appellant has exaggerated the Fulani's motive and means for locating him. I find no instances in the documentation for the existence of any network whereby Fulani herdsmen have tracked down any particular individual in Port Harcourt or elsewhere.

The Fulani conflict is largely concentrated in the North Central and North East region with some incidents in other states including "Delta, Edo, Ekiti, Kaduna and Kogi."27 While there have been reports of the conflict affecting more than 20 states, they are mainly concentrated in five states: Adamawa, Plateau, Tabara, Nasarawa and Benue.28 While I accept that the groups on both sides perpetrate violence, I find the Fulani's area of influence does not extend to Port Harcourt.29 Accordingly, I find that the evidence is not sufficient to establish the presence of Fulani Herdsmen in Port Harcourt such that they would pose a section 96 or 97 risk to the Appellants.

Having found no evidence of the Fulani being able to locate or otherwise pose a risk to the Appellant's in Port Harcourt, I see no merit to the Appellants assertion they would have to live in hiding. The evidence does not support this contention.

The Appellant's further argue that the RPD's rejection of the Appellants' reasons why Port Harcourt would not be a viable IFA seems to suggest it was holding the Appellants to a higher standard of proof than required. I see no basis for this argument. The mere fact that the RPD did not accept the Appellant's explanations does not show it imposed an inappropriately high standard of proof.

For these reasons, I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellants have not established that they would face a serious possibility of persecution, nor a risk to life, danger of torture, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, on a balance of probabilities, in Port Harcourt, from the Fulani Herdsmen.
The Appellants fail on the first prong of the test. IFA in Port Harcourt is not unreasonable or unduly harsh
I find the Appellants also fail on the test's second prong.

The Appellants argue that it would be unduly harsh for them to relocate to Port Harcourt as it would be impossible for the Principal Appellant to obtain employment. In support, the Appellants refer to a publication of the National Bureau of Statistics-Vanguard News Nigeria which indicates unemployment has substantially increased in Nigeria in 2018.

While the Appellants have not produced this document, I nonetheless take note of the fact that unemployment is a serious issue throughout the country, including in Port Harcourt, and is one of the main drivers of migration from Nigeria.30
The Appellants assert they have "no prospects for getting employment" that would provide money for accommodation, medical needs or their children.31

However, the Principal Appellant and his wife both have university degrees - he a BSc in Business Administration, she a BA in Mass Communication. They both have significant employment histories in Nigeria in addition to owning their farm. They both speak English which is in common use throughout Nigeria, including Port HarcourtHarcourt. Given this I do not find that the Appellants would be at any particular disadvantage in seeking employment in Port Harcourt.
Although the Appellants have made no submissions in this regard, I have also considered the psychotherapist's report as it pertains to the reasonableness of the proposed IFA.

I am prepared to accept the report's conclusion that the Principal Appellant is suffering from XXXX XXXX XXXX. However, the Appellants have produced no evidence to show the Principal Appellant would not be unable to obtain adequate treatment in Port Harcourt.

Many Nigerians rely on the private health care sector, which is expensive.32 However, this does not mean that treatment is not available - whether in the public or private system. In fact, the same document indicates that "[m]uch of the healthcare infrastructure is confined to major cities, with people living in urban areas getting four times as much access to healthcare as those living elsewhere."33 Based on this I am unable to conclude that the Appellants would face any undue hardship accessing health care in an urban area such as Port Harcourt.

The Federal Court has held that the threshold for the "objectively unreasonable" standard requires, at a minimum, the proof, through actual and concrete evidence, of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of the Appellant in relocating to a safe area.34 I find that the Appellant has not provided such evidence, and, as such, the RPD was correct in finding that it would not be unreasonable for the Appellant to relocate to Port Harcourt.
For these reasons, the Appellants have failed to show, on a balance, that seeking refuge in Port Harcourt would be unreasonable or unduly harsh.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
